title: Taxes: How They Work
blurb: Gross vs net, brackets, sales tax and what to do with side income.
cards: i
Why taxes exist

Taxes are the price of living in a society that provides shared things: roads, schools, hospitals, police, pensions and emergency services. Nobody could build those alone.

You will pay tax in different ways, often without noticing. Some is taken from your pay before you see it. Some is added to the price of what you buy. Understanding both is the first step to keeping more of what you earn, legally.
i
The main types of tax

Four types cover most of what young people meet:

- **Income tax:** a share of what you earn, usually taken from your pay automatically.
- **Social or pension contributions:** money set aside for retirement, health care or unemployment support.
- **Sales tax (VAT, GST or similar):** added to the price of goods and services. You pay it when you buy.
- **Property and local taxes:** paid by people who own property or live in certain areas.

Rules and rates differ by country, so always check your local tax authority for the exact numbers.
i
Gross, net and withholding

**Gross pay** is the full amount your employer agrees to pay you. **Net pay** is what reaches your bank account after deductions.

Most employers use **withholding**: they calculate your tax and contributions each pay period and send them to the authorities for you. That is why a job can feel simple. You never touch that money.

The gap between gross and net is often 15% to 35%, depending on where you live and how much you earn. Always plan your life around net pay.

Worked example: how tax brackets work

A simple system, using made-up numbers: the first 1,000 of monthly income is taxed at 0%, the next 1,000 at 10%, and anything above 2,000 at 20%. You earn 2,500 a month.

1. First 1,000 × 0% = 0
2. Next 1,000 × 10% = 100
3. Last 500 × 20% = 100
4. Total tax = 200

Your **effective rate** is 200 ÷ 2,500 = 8%, even though your top bracket is 20%.
i
The raise myth

Many people fear a raise could push them into a higher bracket and leave them with less. That cannot happen in a bracket system. Only the slice of income above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate.

In the example above, a 100 raise leaves you 80 better off after tax (100 minus 20% of 100). More pay is always more take-home.

What can cut your take-home are cliffs in benefits or allowances, which depend on your country. If you are close to one, check the rules before assuming.
i
Sales tax and the real price

Sales tax is added to the shelf price in some countries and already included in others. If the price is 200 and sales tax is 15%, you pay 200 × 1.15 = 230.

To take tax out of a price that already includes it, divide instead: 230 ÷ 1.15 = 200. This helps when comparing prices across shops or countries.
i
Side income and self-employment

If you earn money outside a payslip (tutoring, design, reselling, content), nobody withholds tax for you. In most places you must declare it and pay on the profit.

A safe habit: move 20% to 30% of every payment into a separate account the moment you are paid. Keep invoices and receipts. At tax time you will have the money ready and the records to prove your costs.

Rules vary, and small amounts are sometimes exempt, so check your local authority's website.
d
What would you do?
You were paid 800 for a weekend design job. Nothing was withheld.
Spend it all on a new phone
You enjoy the phone, but at tax time you owe money you no longer have. Set aside a share first.
Move about a quarter into a tax pot, keep your records, and spend the rest
Smart. The tax bill is covered and you still have money to enjoy.
Say nothing and hope nobody notices
In most places side income must be declared, and penalties cost more than the tax. Honesty is cheaper.
i
Mistakes to avoid

- Budgeting with gross pay instead of net pay.
- Spending side income without setting tax aside.
- Throwing away payslips and receipts.
- Ignoring letters from the tax authority. Deadlines and penalties are real.
- Believing a large refund is a bonus. It usually means you overpaid during the year and lent the government your money for free.
- Paying anyone who contacts you saying you owe tax. Real authorities do not demand gift cards or instant transfers.

Net pay is the number to budget with.
Brackets tax slices of income, so a raise never lowers take-home pay.
Your effective rate is lower than your top bracket rate.
Sales tax is added at the till. Multiply to add it, divide to remove it.
Side income usually needs declaring: set aside 20% to 30% and keep records.
q
You earn 2,400 gross. Tax and contributions take 480. What can you safely budget with?
Net pay = 2,400 − 480 = 1,920. Budget with the money that actually arrives.
q
Using the example brackets (0% to 1,000, 10% to 2,000, 20% above), how much tax is due on 2,500?
0 + 100 + 100 = 200, an effective rate of 8%.

You are paid 1,000 for a freelance job and nobody withheld tax. What is the smartest first move?
Spend it before you forget
Move a share (about 20% to 30%) to a separate tax pot
Hide it from the authorities
Lend it to a friend
Setting money aside immediately means the tax bill never becomes a crisis.
t
A big tax refund is a free bonus from the government.
A refund means too much was withheld. You overpaid and got your own money back, with no interest.
q
Someone calls saying you owe tax and must pay today with gift cards. What is this?
Normal procedure
A scam
A refund
An error by your bank
Real tax authorities do not demand gift cards or instant transfers. Hang up and contact them using official contact details.
